4.1.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables in an investigation.
Decide how to change the independent variable over a suitable range.
Decide how many values to measure at, and where to take more.
Decide how to identify a biological molecule and estimate its quantity by standardising a test.
Describe an appropriate control and the variables to standardise.
Decide which variables to standardise and how.
Decide and describe how to measure the dependent variable accurately and precisely.
Decide whether to repeat or replicate readings, and why.
Follow instructions or diagrams for a range of techniques to collect results.
Assess the risk of a procedure as low, medium or high.
Take accurate readings with a range of apparatus.
Record qualitative results, such as colour changes, in clear terms.

4.2.text: Set up a light microscope to make plan diagrams or cell drawings.
Stain and mount a slide of cells.
Calibrate an eyepiece graticule against a stage micrometer.
Find actual sizes of tissues or cells with a calibrated graticule, as a mean, in micrometres.
Estimate the number of cells or organelles in a field of view or slide.
Draw a plan diagram: tissue layers in correct proportion and no cells.
Draw the observable features of cells: shapes, cell walls, relative sizes and observable contents only.
Compare two specimens using only observable features.
Make clear, unshaded drawings with sharp, unbroken lines that use the space available.
Show every step in graticule, actual-size, magnification, count-per-area, mean and ratio calculations.
Compare observable features of slides and photomicrographs.
Use biological knowledge to explain observations, calculated values and how a specimen is adapted to its habitat.

4.3.text: Record raw data in a fully ruled table with no units in the body.
Head table columns with the quantity and unit, independent variable first.
Record measurements to the same number of significant figures, set by the instrument.
Show every step and the reasoning in a calculation.
Give calculated values to the same number of significant figures as, or one more than, the least accurate measurement.
Choose between a graph and a chart, then present it clearly and accurately.
Put the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis, both labelled with units.
Choose scales that use most of the grid and can be read easily.
Plot every point accurately as a small cross or dot in a circle.
Join plotted points correctly: line of best fit, smooth curve or ruled straight lines, without extrapolating.
Draw bars separated for discrete or categorical data and joined for continuous data.

4.4.text: Calculate an answer to the correct number of significant figures from results or data.
Find an unknown value from graph coordinates, intercepts or extrapolation.
Estimate the concentration of an unknown solution from qualitative results.
Identify the contents of an unknown solution using biological molecule tests.
Identify anomalous results and leave them out before calculating a mean.
Describe patterns and trends in tables and graphs, using the data.
Identify systematic and random errors and say how each affects results.
Identify the significant sources of error in an investigation.
Calculate actual and percentage error and judge confidence in the results.
Judge how standardising variables affects confidence in a conclusion.
Predict a trend from information or results provided.
Draw a conclusion from the patterns and trends in data.
Decide whether data support a given hypothesis.
Draw a conclusion from results, including estimating an unknown concentration from known ones.
Explain data, observations, calculated values and conclusions using biological knowledge.
Suggest improvements that make the procedure or the observations more accurate.
Suggest how to modify or extend an investigation to answer a new question.

5.1.text: Work with averages, decimals, fractions, percentages, ratios and reciprocals.
Use decimal and standard form, including negative powers of ten.
Use the prefixes giga, mega, kilo, milli, micro and nano.
Keep significant figures justified: not lost early, not carried too far.
Express errors in experimental work as percentage errors.

5.2.text: Draw charts and graphs from given data.
Select suitable scales and axes for a graph.
Construct and interpret frequency distributions, pie charts, bar charts and histograms.
Choose between a bar chart, histogram and line graph.
Decide between ruled straight lines and a line of best fit.
Calculate a rate of change from a graph line.
Draw and use a tangent to a curve to find a rate of change.
Translate information between graphical, numerical and algebraic forms.

5.3.text: Use the relationship between length, surface area and volume and their units.
Calculate areas, circumferences, surface areas and volumes of simple shapes.
Use Simpson's Index of Diversity to calculate and interpret biodiversity.
